subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 14 periods = 560 minutes
Total: 14 periods · 9h 20min

periods.activity_title: First Read: Water Storage Across India

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students what they know about water storage. Students share briefly — wells, taps, tanks — building an anchor in familiar experience before the text is opened.

Teacher reads the full informational text aloud (Textbook pp.65–68), pausing at each new structure — Oorani, Panam Keni, Tanka, overhead tank — to show the location on the India map and invite a one-word reaction from students.
Students echo-read two paragraphs — the one on Punjab's sculpted tanks — following the teacher's pacing and intonation aloud together as a class.
Teacher poses one closing question: 'What surprised you most in this text?' Two or three students share their response aloud before the unit ends.

periods.teacher_notes: The text introduces four distinct water storage structures across different Indian regions — pace the read-aloud slowly enough for students to absorb the geography. Students may conflate Oorani, Panam Keni, and Tanka as 'the same kind of well'; name each explicitly and note the region when reading.
materials: India map (wall chart or textbook map)

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion: Tanks and Their Stories

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.68): answer questions on water tanks and Punjab tank shapes.

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to recall, without opening their books, the names of the four water storage structures described in the text. This re-activates the key content before questions are explored.

Class discusses 'Let us Think — A.' questions 1 and 2 (p.68) orally. Teacher elicits answers, probes reasoning ('Why does the text say tanks serve more than one purpose?'), and confirms with a shared-reading of the relevant paragraph.

Class discusses questions 3 and 4 (p.68) — construction of Punjab tanks and how shapes reflect owners' identities. Teacher uses the text's examples (rooster, tractor, aeroplane) and asks students which design they would choose for their own home and why.
Students write answers to all four 'Let us Think — A.' questions independently in their notebooks. Teacher circulates to support sentence formation.
Two students read their answers aloud. Teacher affirms accurate responses and gently corrects any factual confusion about which region uses which structure.

periods.teacher_notes: The question about Punjab's tank shapes (question 4) often draws vague answers; prompt students to quote from the text — 'a farmer who loves tractors' or 'a football fan' — rather than generalising. Watch for students who confuse steel frame (the structural element) with the cement finish (the sculpting surface).

periods.activity_title: Thinking Aloud: Water Storage and Our Choices

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — B. (p.68): oral discussion on other water storage methods and personal tank designs.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reminds students of the text's description of Ooranis, Panam Keni, Tankas, and overhead tanks. This re-anchors the content before students extend it through their own experience.

Class takes up 'Let us Think — B.' question 1 (p.68): students share other water storage methods they know — ponds, dams, earthen pots, rainwater harvesting barrels. Teacher lists responses on the board and links each briefly to the text's structures where relevant.

Students respond to question 2 (p.68): if they were to build a water tank, what shape would they choose and why? Students first think silently for one minute, then share with a partner, then three or four students share with the full class. Teacher notes the variety of reasons — personal passion, family occupation, favourite animal — mirroring the text's logic.

Teacher draws the conversation together: 'The text says these tanks are cultural expressions — what does that mean, based on what you just said?' Two students respond in a full sentence before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may list modern appliances (water purifiers, bottles) rather than storage structures; guide them toward structures that hold water for future use, which is the text's frame. Encourage shy students by offering a sentence starter: 'I would build a tank shaped like a ___ because ___.'

periods.activity_title: Group Discussion: Water Wastage and Solutions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak — A. (pp.73–74): group discussion on water wastage and ways to stop it.

homework.task_brief: Let us Speak — B. (p.74): write three examples of water wastage and solutions in notebook.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the example from 'Let us Speak — A.' (pp.73–74) aloud: 'Using running water to brush teeth wastes water; a tumbler saves it.' Students identify the two parts — wastage and solution — before groups begin.

Students sit in groups of three and discuss the two prompts: how water is wasted daily, and what can stop each waste. Each group generates at least three examples. Teacher circulates, prompting quieter members and nudging groups that stall.
Each group nominates one speaker to share their examples with the class. Teacher records the clearest examples on the board, creating a shared class list of wastage-solution pairs.

Teacher closes the unit by connecting the discussion back to the text: 'The ancient Tankas and Ooranis exist because people understood scarcity — what does our list today say about our own understanding?'

periods.teacher_notes: Groups often rush to obvious examples like leaving taps running; encourage them to think beyond the bathroom — water used in cooking, gardening, or washing vehicles. The homework item asks students to write three examples from the class discussion in their own words, so the board list supports them.

periods.activity_title: Sound Play: 'What a Tank!' and Homophones

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak — C. (p.74): say aloud and compare 'What a tank!' / 'Water tank' and 'I scream' / 'Ice cream'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher says 'What a tank!' and 'Water tank' aloud twice each at normal speed, then asks students to listen carefully: do the two phrases sound the same when spoken quickly? Students raise hands to vote yes or no.

Class works through 'Let us Speak — C.' (p.74) together. Teacher leads choral repetition of both pairs — 'What a tank!' / 'Water tank' and 'I scream' / 'Ice cream' — several times, then students discuss the four questions in the task (same word? same meaning? same sound? same meaning?) with a partner.

Pairs share their answers. Teacher guides the class toward the key insight: two phrases can sound almost identical yet mean entirely different things. Students suggest additional pairs from their own experience if they can.
Students practise saying each pair in a sentence of their own — 'What a tank they built in Punjab!' and 'The water tank is full.' — repeating with a partner for clear articulation and stress.
Teacher names the phenomenon simply — words and phrases that sound alike but mean differently — and invites one student to explain it in their own words as a closing sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: The insight that identical sounds can carry entirely different meanings is the core of this task; do not rush to the label before students have heard the difference themselves. 'I scream' / 'Ice cream' is the more dramatic pair and often unlocks genuine delight — let students enjoy it before moving on.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (pp.74–75): listen to 'A Day without Water' and answer five multiple-choice questions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets up the listening: 'You are about to hear a story about a girl called Suma who woke up one morning to find no water. Listen carefully — you will answer questions about what happened.' Students close their textbooks.

Teacher reads the passage 'A Day without Water' (pp.74–75) aloud at a clear, steady pace — three full readings. Students listen without writing during the first two readings; on the third, they may jot one or two key words.
Students open their textbooks to p.75 and work through the five 'Let us Listen' multiple-choice questions independently. Teacher re-reads any portion of the passage once if students request.
Teacher goes through each question aloud, inviting students to share their chosen answer and the part of the story that supports it. Incorrect choices are gently traced back to the passage.
Teacher closes with: 'Suma promised something at the end of the story — what was it, and why does it connect to what we read about Tankas and Ooranis?' One student responds before the unit ends.

periods.teacher_notes: Three readings is the NCF preparatory guidance for listening tasks; resist the temptation to read a fourth time — the productive challenge is part of the task. Students who struggle with MCQ format may need a reminder that they are choosing one best answer, not writing a sentence.

periods.activity_title: Contractions: Shortening Words with an Apostrophe

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.69): write contractions for six 'not' pairs.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes on the board: 'aren't' and 'are not'. Students discuss what changed — which letters disappeared and what replaced them. Teacher introduces the term contraction and the apostrophe's role, using the text's own example from the chapter.

Class works through 'Let us Learn — A.' (p.69) together: teacher reads each pair aloud ('do not' → ?), students chorally say the contraction, then write it in their notebooks. Teacher writes each answer on the board immediately after students respond.

Students attempt the six items independently in their notebooks, covering the board answers. Teacher circulates and checks apostrophe placement — the most common error at this stage is omitting the apostrophe or placing it after the 'n'.
Class self-checks against the board list. Students who got all six correct help a partner who did not by pointing to where the missing letters were.

Teacher reads two sentences from the informational text (pp.65–68) aloud, one containing a contraction in natural context, and asks students to identify it. This closes the unit by grounding the rule in real text.

periods.teacher_notes: The commonest error is 'ca'nt' (apostrophe placed between 'a' and 'n') rather than 'can't' (between 'n' and 't'); write the correct form large on the board and keep it visible throughout. 'Cannot' is one word, not two, so 'can not' → 'can't' needs brief explanation.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (p.69): rewrite paragraphs 1 and 2, replacing underlined words with contractions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the six contractions formed in the previous work with contractions — 'don't', 'isn't', 'aren't', 'can't', 'couldn't', 'didn't' — by pointing to them on the board or having students call them out. This re-establishes the forms before they appear embedded in a paragraph.
Teacher reads paragraph 1 of 'Let us Learn — B.' (p.69) aloud, pausing at each underlined word. Students identify the underlined form and call out the contraction together before anyone writes.
Students rewrite paragraph 1 in their notebooks, replacing all underlined words with contractions. Teacher circulates and prompts where students stall, but does not give the answer outright.
Students rewrite paragraph 2 independently. Teacher notes on the board any contraction that is causing repeated errors across the class and addresses it briefly before the class self-checks.
Two students read their completed rewritten paragraphs aloud. The class listens for any contraction that still sounds wrong. Teacher confirms the final correct forms.

periods.teacher_notes: Paragraph 2 contains 'does not', which produces 'doesn't' — a form not in the A-task list, so students encounter it fresh here; write it on the board when it arises rather than anticipating it. Students who copy the paragraphs out without substituting are a common observation — circulate early to catch this.

periods.activity_title: Exclamatory Sentences and Animal Family Names

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — C. (p.70): read, identify, and name emotions in exclamatory sentences.
Let us Learn — E. (p.71): read and study animal family name sets with illustrations.

homework.task_brief: Let us Learn — D. (p.70): find five exclamatory sentences from Grade 4 textbook and record emotions in a table.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the three exclamatory sentences in 'Let us Learn — C.' (p.70) aloud with exaggerated expression. Students identify what emotion each one expresses and the class names four emotions together. Teacher connects the exclamation mark to the feeling it signals.

Students look at the five animal family illustrations in 'Let us Learn — E.' (p.71). Teacher reads each row aloud: 'lion – lioness – lion cub'. Students repeat chorally, then cover the text and the teacher points to an illustration, students call out all three family members from memory.

Students practise the animal family names in pairs — one student says the male form, the other supplies the female and young. Teacher circulates and focuses on the less familiar sets: stallion–mare–foal and bull–cow–calf.

Teacher asks students to compose one exclamatory sentence using one of the animal names from the E-task. Two or three students share aloud: 'What a beautiful mare!' confirms both skills working together.

Homework for the D-task is set: students are asked to find five exclamatory sentences from their Grade 4 English textbook and note the feeling expressed in each, recording them in a two-column table in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: The C-task and E-task are independent pieces of vocabulary work and can be treated as two separate episodes within the unit — do not try to link them artificially. For E, the rooster–hen–chick set connects back to the sculpted Punjab tanks described in the chapter, which can serve as a brief bridge.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (pp.72–73): design a poster to preserve and clean old water tanks, including a slogan, bullet points, and an invitation.

time_bands.activity: Teacher discusses what a poster must do — catch the eye, say something important briefly, tell the reader what to do next. Together the class identifies the four required elements from 'Let us Write — A.' (pp.72–73): topic, slogan, bullet points on importance of tanks, and an invitation with place and time.

Teacher models a partial poster on the board: writes the topic heading, then thinks aloud while composing one slogan ('Save Tanks, Save Lives!' is the textbook example — teacher makes a different one to model originality). Two bullet points are drafted together as a class.

Students independently draft their own poster in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, reads drafts, and gives brief verbal feedback — 'Your slogan is strong; now add a specific time and place for the drive.' Students revise on the spot.
Three students read their slogans aloud. Class votes on the most memorable and briefly explains why — connecting to what makes a slogan effective.

Teacher notes that the poster draws on everything the chapter taught — the value of water tanks, community responsibility, and conservation — and closes by asking students to check that all four required elements are present in their drafts.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often write the slogan last and as an afterthought; the modelling step should make it the first and most creative element so they give it proper thought. Bullet points about tank importance should draw on the text's content — ancient structures, flood prevention, community unity — rather than generic water-saving tips.

periods.activity_title: Word Families: Endings that Make Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — B. (p.73): write ten words each ending in '-er', '-or', and '-at'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'water' on the board and asks students to notice how it ends. Students call out other words ending in '-er' from their own vocabulary. Teacher lists five on the board as a class warm-up before the task begins.

Students work on the '-er' column of 'Let us Write — B.' (p.73) independently in their notebooks, aiming for ten words. Teacher circulates and encourages students who stall to think by category — animals, jobs, kitchen objects — that naturally end in '-er'.
Students move on to '-or' words. Teacher writes one model (e.g. 'doctor') and asks students to think of job-related words, which is the most productive category for this ending.
Students complete the '-at' column. This ending yields short, concrete words (mat, hat, bat, flat, that); teacher encourages students to look at rhyming families rather than random recall.
Each student shares their one most unusual word from any column. Teacher notes repeated or favourite words on the board. Students add any new words from classmates to their own lists.

periods.teacher_notes: The '-or' column is typically the hardest because students conflate it with '-er' (e.g. 'teacher' not 'teacor'); focus on words where the '-or' spelling is the standard form, such as occupational nouns. This task builds vocabulary range through pattern-awareness rather than memorisation.

periods.activity_title: Research and Chart: How Are Water Tanks Cleaned?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore — A. (p.77): find out and chart tank-cleaning techniques; present to class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a question: 'The text describes how tanks are built — but what happens to them over time? What might grow or collect inside?' Students speculate briefly: algae, sediment, rust, bacteria. Teacher affirms and frames the unit's inquiry: how are tanks cleaned?

Students work in pairs to brainstorm what they already know or can logically deduce about tank-cleaning steps. Each pair writes their ideas on a half-sheet of paper. Teacher circulates, prompting with questions: 'Do you drain it first? What tools might be needed?'

Each pair shares their ideas. Teacher synthesises the responses into a class chart on the board with two columns: 'Step' and 'Why it matters'. Students copy the class chart into their notebooks, adding any pictures or diagrams they can sketch.

Students discuss: 'Which of these steps matters most for keeping water safe to drink, and why?' One or two students give a short oral response. Teacher links this back to the chapter's celebration of tanks as vital community structures.

Teacher invites students to note one question they still have about tank maintenance — something they would like to find out at home or at the library — and reads two of these aloud to close the unit with curiosity intact.

periods.teacher_notes: Students will not have researched tank-cleaning techniques before arriving; this unit is designed to work from logical inference and prior common sense, not from pre-gathered materials. If any student has seen a tank being cleaned at home, their account is valuable primary knowledge — invite it early.

periods.activity_title: The Thirsty Crow: Enactment and Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore — B. (p.78): enact the Thirsty Crow school-visit event using the picture sequence.

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows the four sequential pictures of The Thirsty Crow (p.78) and invites the class to narrate the story aloud together, one picture at a time. Students supply the key action for each frame without prompting.

Teacher frames the enactment: the school has invited the crow to a student interaction. The class assigns roles — the crow, a student interviewer, two or three audience members with questions. Students plan their lines briefly in pairs before performing.

Two or three groups enact the interaction in front of the class. Each enactment runs to its own natural end. Audience members ask at least one genuine question to the 'crow' about its problem-solving method.

Class discusses the link between the crow's solution and the chapter's theme: both involve finding a way to get or store water through ingenuity. Students articulate this connection in a sentence before the discussion closes.

Teacher closes the unit: 'Whether it is a crow dropping pebbles or a community building an Oorani, the instinct to solve a water problem is very old — and very human.' Students note one sentence of reflection in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: The Thirsty Crow is a familiar story for most Grade V students; the novelty is the enactment frame of a school interview, which asks students to imagine the crow as a guest speaker rather than a story character. Keep the enactment playful — humour is appropriate here and helps quieter students participate.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Water, Ingenuity, and Expression

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a mind-map on the board labelled 'What a Tank!' and draws five branches: Traditional Structures, Modern Tanks, Punjab's Art Tanks, Water Conservation, and Language. Students call out one word or phrase for each branch from everything the chapter covered. Teacher populates the map from their responses.

Students take turns retelling the chapter's main ideas orally — one student describes the traditional structures, another the Punjab tanks, a third the link to conservation — building a collaborative spoken summary. Teacher ensures each strand of the text is voiced before moving on.

Quick word-work game: teacher calls out a full form ('would not', 'is not', 'did not') and students race to write the contraction on their personal white board or notebook. Teacher then calls out an animal name ('tigress', 'foal', 'hen') and students call back the full family set. This revisits both vocabulary strands in a brisk, game-like format.

Students write three to four sentences in their notebooks responding to this synthesis prompt: 'The informational text and the Thirsty Crow story both celebrate the same human quality — what is it, and how do you see it in each?' Students write independently; teacher circulates without intervening.

Three students read their written responses aloud. The class listens for the quality named — ingenuity, resourcefulness, or care for water — and whether the student named it in both the text and the story. Teacher draws threads together on the board.

Teacher closes the chapter: 'From a Tanka in the Thar to a sculpted rooster on a rooftop in Punjab — this chapter showed us that how people hold water tells us something about who they are.' No further task is set.

periods.teacher_notes: The synthesis draws on the informational text's content about traditional and modern water storage, Punjab's artistic tanks, the conservation discussion, contractions and animal family vocabulary, and The Thirsty Crow enactment — all by naming the ideas, not by assuming any particular activity happened. Students who engage deeply with the writing prompt typically connect ingenuity as the thread; accept resourcefulness, creativity, or care for water as equally valid.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has correctly identified Tanka but wrongly placed it in Tamil Nadu and confused its function with Oorani's rainwater harvesting role.

options.label: B
options.text: She promised to tell her friends about saving water.

options.label: C

options.label: D

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have confused Suma's general awareness with a specific habit she mentioned.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has recalled a later action (telling friends) and mistaken it for the promise.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has invented a detail not present in the listening passage.
